metadata.description: What actually happens inside a Docker build: how per-instruction layer caching works and why instruction order matters, why multi-stage builds discard the heavy toolchain so only the final output ships, how CI-level dependency caching (keyed off a lockfile hash) differs from Docker's own layer cache, how container vulnerability scanning checks image layers against CVE databases, and why both caching and scanning have to be designed-in steps rather than afterthoughts.

beats.narration_text: This week's learning focus was understanding what actually happens inside a Docker build — how layers and caching work, and how container images are checked for security vulnerabilities.

props.segment: Week 9 Technical Learnings — Docker Layers, Caching & Scanning
props.runningText: layer caching → multi-stage builds → CI caching → vulnerability scanning…
output: what actually happens inside a Docker build
layers, caching, and image security together

beats.role_note: slide 2 -- per-instruction caching, why order matters
beats.narration_text: Every instruction in a Dockerfile — each COPY, RUN, or FROM — caches each layer individually. If a layer's inputs haven't changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached version instead of re-executing it. This is why instruction order matters: putting steps that change often, like copying source code, after steps that rarely change, maximizes how much of the build can be served from cache.

nodes.d: reused if inputs haven't changed since last build

nodes.k: Stacked on top of the last
nodes.d: order matters — volatile steps go last

props.caption: Putting source code copies after rarely-changing steps maximizes what's served from cache.

beats.role_note: slide 3 -- heavy toolchain discarded, only output ships
beats.narration_text: A multi-stage build lets you use a full toolchain — compilers, package managers, dev dependencies — in an early stage, and then copy only the final build output into a clean, minimal final stage. Everything from the earlier stage never ships, which is what keeps production images small and reduces what's exposed if the image is ever compromised.

nodes.d: full toolchain — compilers, package managers, dev deps
into a clean, minimal final stage
never ships — smaller image, less exposed if compromised

props.caption: Only the final stage ships — everything used to build it is discarded.

beats.role_note: slide 4 -- dependency caching keyed off a lockfile hash
beats.narration_text: Beyond Docker's own layer caching, CI systems like GitHub Actions can cache dependency installations directly, usually keyed off a hash of the lockfile. If the lockfile hasn't changed, the cached dependencies are restored instantly instead of re-downloading everything — which is one of the highest-leverage ways to speed up a pipeline with very little added complexity.

nodes.d: lockfile changed — install step actually runs

props.caption: High leverage, low complexity — one of the cheapest ways to speed up a pipeline.

beats.role_note: slide 5 -- checking layers against CVE databases
beats.narration_text: Vulnerability scanning works by inspecting every package inside an image's layers — including the base OS and any system libraries — and checking them against databases of publicly known vulnerabilities, called CVEs. Most vulnerabilities in a container don't come from your own application code; they come from inherited base images and system packages that need to be kept current.

nodes.d: usually traced to inherited base images, not app code

props.caption: Most container vulnerabilities are inherited, not written — and need to be kept current.

beats.act: WHY THIS BELONGS IN THE PIPELINE, NOT AFTER IT
beats.narration_text: The real insight this week was that caching and scanning both need to be designed-in steps, not afterthoughts — caching has to be designed into the build order from the start to be effective, and scanning has to run before deployment to actually prevent a vulnerable image from going live, rather than just reporting on one that already did.

nodes.d: actually prevents a vulnerable image going live

nodes.k: Not an audit after the fact
nodes.d: reporting on an image that already shipped is too late

props.caption: Scan integrated before deploy, not as a separate audit later.

beats.role_note: slide 7 -- the closing line, Claude cream skin
beats.narration_text: Understanding layers, caching, and scanning together is what turns Docker from 'a way to package the app' into a deliberate, efficient, and secure part of the delivery pipeline.

props.artifactHeading: A well-designed container build is fast and safe by design.
artifactLines: Layers: each Dockerfile instruction caches individually — instruction order decides what's reusable.
Multi-stage builds: the full toolchain is discarded — only the final, minimal output ships.
CI caching: dependencies restore instantly on a lockfile-hash cache hit, instead of re-downloading.
Scanning: image layers are checked against CVE databases — most findings are inherited, not written.
Both caching and scanning are designed-in steps, not afterthoughts bolted on later.
